passages.title: Low-emission zones
passages.text: Several European cities have introduced low-emission zones that keep older diesel vehicles out of the centre. Supporters point to measured falls in nitrogen dioxide along major roads within the first year. Critics argue that the zones move traffic to surrounding districts rather than reducing it, and that owners of older vehicles, often on lower incomes, bear most of the cost. Some cities offer grants towards a replacement vehicle or a public transport pass, although take-up has varied widely. Evaluations so far have focused mainly on air quality; fewer have looked at journeys or household budgets.

passages.title: Remote work and office space
passages.text: Since remote working became widespread, many public administrations have reviewed how much office space they need. Occupancy surveys in several administrations show that buildings are now busiest from Tuesday to Thursday and almost empty on Mondays and Fridays. Some organisations have responded by introducing shared desks, while others have kept assigned desks but given up whole floors. Managers report that shared desks save money but can make it harder for new staff to find colleagues. Few organisations have yet measured whether productivity has changed, so decisions are being made largely on the basis of cost and staff preferences.

passages.title: Date labels on food
passages.text: Food packaging in the EU carries one of two date labels. A 'use by' date relates to safety: after it, food such as fresh meat or fish should not be eaten, even if it looks and smells fine. A 'best before' date relates to quality: after it, food such as pasta, rice or biscuits may lose some flavour or texture but is still safe if it has been stored properly. Surveys suggest that many consumers do not know the difference and throw away food that is still safe to eat. For this reason, reducing confusion over date labels is often presented as a simple way to cut household food waste.

passages.title: Online public consultations
passages.text: Public authorities increasingly invite citizens to comment on draft laws through online consultations. The method is cheap and open to anyone with an internet connection, and it can gather thousands of responses in a few weeks. However, responses tend to come from people and organisations who already follow the subject closely, so they may not reflect the views of the wider public. Some authorities therefore combine online consultations with smaller panels of randomly selected citizens. When a consultation receives a large number of identical responses, these are usually treated as a single organised campaign rather than counted individually.

passages.title: The return of night trains
passages.text: Overnight rail services, many of which were withdrawn in the early 2000s, are returning on several European routes. Operators argue that a night train saves travellers both a hotel night and the time lost getting to and from airports. Demand has been strongest on routes of between 800 and 1,500 kilometres, which are too long for a comfortable day journey by train but short enough to cover overnight. The services remain difficult to run profitably, however: sleeping cars carry fewer passengers than seated carriages, and each train can make only one journey per night. Several routes therefore depend on support from public authorities.

passages.title: Urban meadows
passages.text: A number of towns have stopped mowing parts of their parks and roadside verges every few weeks and now cut them only once or twice a year. The longer grass allows wild flowers to grow, which provide food for bees and other pollinating insects. Councils that have made the change report lower maintenance costs, as fewer cuts are needed. Not all residents approve: some regard the uncut areas as untidy, and councils have received complaints about long grass near paths and playgrounds. Many towns now leave a mown strip along the edges of uncut areas to show that the grass has been left long deliberately.

passages.title: E-books in public libraries
passages.text: Most public libraries now lend e-books as well as printed books. Unlike a printed book, which a library buys once and can lend for as long as it lasts, an e-book is usually licensed from the publisher. Many licences expire after a fixed period, often two years, or after a set number of loans, after which the library must pay again. Libraries argue that these terms make e-books far more expensive to provide than printed copies. Publishers reply that unlimited lending of digital copies, which never wear out, could reduce sales to readers. Some countries have begun negotiating national agreements on prices and terms on behalf of all their libraries.

passages.title: Repair cafés
passages.text: Repair cafés are free events at which volunteers help people fix broken household items, from toasters to bicycles. Visitors are expected to take part in the repair rather than simply hand the item over, so that they learn how to deal with similar faults in future. Organisers record what is brought in and whether it was fixed; across many events, roughly half of all items leave in working order. The most common obstacles are parts that are glued or riveted together and spare parts that are no longer sold. Several organisers have shared their records with policymakers working on rules that would make products easier to repair.

passages.title: Changing the clocks
passages.text: Twice a year, clocks in most European countries move forward or back by one hour. The practice was introduced mainly to save energy, but studies now suggest that the savings are small, partly because lighting accounts for a smaller share of energy use than it once did. Critics also point to disrupted sleep in the days after each change. Ending the changes is not straightforward, however: each country would have to choose whether to stay on summer or winter time permanently, and neighbouring countries choosing differently could create new time differences for travellers and businesses.

passages.title: Plain language in official letters
passages.text: Letters from public authorities are often written in long sentences full of legal terms. Several administrations have tested rewriting such letters in plain language, using shorter sentences, everyday words and a clear statement of what the reader must do and by when. In these trials, the rewritten letters led to fewer phone calls asking for explanations and more replies sent on time. Plain language does not mean leaving out legal details: these can still be included, for example in a separate section. The main cost is the time needed to rewrite and test standard letters, which officials say is recovered through the reduction in queries.

passages.title: Rental e-scooters
passages.text: Rental electric scooters appeared in many European cities with little warning, as operators placed hundreds of them on the streets overnight. Users welcomed a quick way to cover short distances, but pedestrians complained about scooters left on pavements. Cities responded in different ways. Some limited the number of operators through a tender, some required scooters to be parked in marked bays, and a few banned rental scooters altogether. Data from operators suggest that most trips are under three kilometres and that many replace walking rather than car journeys, which weakens the claim that scooters significantly cut traffic emissions.

passages.title: Seasonal farm work
passages.text: Farms that grow fruit and vegetables need many extra workers for a few weeks at harvest time. Much of this work is done by seasonal workers who travel from other regions or countries. Employers say that finding enough workers has become harder, as fewer people are willing to do physically demanding work for short periods. Some farms have invested in machines, but delicate crops such as strawberries and asparagus are still largely picked by hand. Workers' organisations point out that housing provided by employers is not always of an acceptable standard and call for more regular inspections.

passages.title: Managed retreat from the coast
passages.text: Along some stretches of coast, the sea is eroding the land by several metres a year. Traditionally, authorities have defended such coasts with sea walls and rock barriers. These defences are expensive to build and maintain, and they can increase erosion further along the coast by blocking the natural movement of sand. In a few places, authorities have instead chosen 'managed retreat': allowing the sea to flood low-lying land in a controlled way, which can create salt marshes that absorb wave energy. Managed retreat is often opposed by people whose land or homes would be lost, and compensation schemes are rarely considered generous.

passages.title: Interpreting in meetings
passages.text: In meetings where participants speak different languages, interpreters usually work in soundproof booths and translate speech as it is delivered, a method known as simultaneous interpretation. The work is so demanding that interpreters normally take turns, each speaking for about half an hour at a time. Speakers can help by sending their texts in advance and by not reading too quickly. Remote interpretation, in which interpreters work from a distance via an online platform, became common during periods when travel was restricted. Interpreters have reported that poor sound quality on such platforms makes their work more tiring.

passages.title: The return of the wolf
passages.text: After being absent for more than a century, wolves have returned to several parts of Western Europe, mostly by moving in from neighbouring areas rather than through reintroduction. Their protected status has allowed numbers to grow. The return is welcomed by many conservationists, but livestock farmers report losses of sheep and goats. Authorities in several regions now pay compensation for animals killed by wolves and subsidise electric fences and guard dogs. Studies suggest that well-maintained fences greatly reduce attacks, although they are costly to install across large or hilly grazing areas.

passages.title: Tourist taxes
passages.text: A growing number of European cities charge visitors a tourist tax, usually a small fixed amount per person per night added to the hotel bill. Supporters argue that visitors should contribute to the cost of services they use, such as street cleaning and public transport. Some cities set higher rates in peak season or for more expensive hotels. Hotel associations have warned that higher taxes could lead visitors to choose other destinations, although cities that have raised their rates have so far reported little effect on visitor numbers. In several cities, the tax now also applies to short-term rentals booked through online platforms.

passages.title: Open data
passages.text: Many public administrations publish data sets online free of charge, from public transport timetables to air quality readings. The aim is to allow businesses, researchers and citizens to reuse the data, for example to build travel apps or to check how public money is spent. Experience shows that publication alone is not enough: data that are out of date, poorly described or released in formats that computers cannot easily read are rarely reused. Administrations that have seen the most reuse tend to update their data regularly and to ask users which data sets they need.

passages.title: Young volunteers
passages.text: Surveys suggest that young people are as willing to volunteer as older generations, but they volunteer in different ways. Rather than committing to a fixed weekly role in one organisation, many prefer short projects that fit around studies and work, often found through online platforms. Some organisations have struggled to adapt, as their activities depend on volunteers who can be relied on for months at a time. Others have split long-term roles into smaller tasks. Volunteering can also help young people gain skills and experience that employers value, which is one reason some schools and universities recognise it formally.

passages.title: Access to cash
passages.text: The share of payments made in cash has fallen steadily as more people pay by card or phone. As a result, banks have closed many branches and cash machines, especially in rural areas, where fewer transactions make them less profitable. Consumer groups warn that this affects people who rely on cash, including some older people and people on low incomes who use it to keep control of their spending. Some countries have introduced rules requiring that cash withdrawal points remain available within a certain distance of most homes. Retailers' views are mixed: cash is costly to handle, but card payments involve fees.

passages.title: The four-day week
passages.text: Several companies and public bodies have trialled a four-day working week, in which staff work fewer hours for the same pay. In most trials, employers report that output stayed broadly the same, and staff report less stress and fewer sick days. Critics note that the organisations taking part volunteered to do so and may therefore be those best suited to the change. They also point out that services which must be staffed continuously, such as hospitals, would need to hire more people to cover the same hours. Many trial participants chose to continue with the shorter week after the trial ended.

passages.title: Self-service libraries
passages.text: Some public libraries now stay open in the early morning and late evening without staff. Registered users enter with their library card, borrow and return books at machines, and use the study spaces, while cameras and a remote alarm service provide security. Libraries that have tried the model report that longer opening hours are popular with students and with people who work during the day. Librarians' unions have raised concerns that unstaffed hours could later be used to justify cutting staffed hours. So far, the libraries concerned have kept their staffed hours unchanged and added the unstaffed hours on top.

passages.title: Protected cycle lanes
passages.text: Many cities have built cycle lanes separated from motor traffic by kerbs or posts, rather than just painted on the road. Counts carried out before and after such lanes opened often show a rise in the number of cyclists on the route, especially among people who had not cycled in traffic before. Local shopkeepers sometimes oppose the lanes because they remove parking spaces in front of their shops. Several studies have found, however, that shoppers who arrive on foot or by bicycle visit more often, even if they spend less on each visit. Whether this makes up for lost parking varies from street to street.

passages.title: Working in extreme heat
passages.text: As summer heat waves become more frequent, several countries have introduced rules for people who work outdoors, such as builders and farm workers. Typical measures include starting work earlier in the day, providing shade and drinking water, and stopping heavy outdoor work when temperatures pass a set level. Employers' organisations generally accept the need for protection but ask for flexibility, since a fixed temperature limit can stop work even where the risk is low. Trade unions argue that without a clear limit, workers may find it hard to refuse dangerous work. Some countries combine a temperature limit with an assessment of each workplace.

passages.title: Learning languages with apps
passages.text: Language-learning apps have attracted millions of users with short daily lessons and game-like rewards. Research suggests that they can help beginners build vocabulary and keep up a regular habit of practice. However, most apps offer few chances to hold a real conversation, and learners who rely on them alone often struggle to speak spontaneously. Many teachers therefore recommend combining an app with lessons or conversation groups. Some apps have responded by adding speaking exercises marked by speech-recognition software, although learners report that these do not always recognise accents accurately.

passages.title: Deposit schemes for bottles
passages.text: In a deposit return scheme, shoppers pay a small extra amount when they buy a drink in a plastic bottle or can and get the money back when they return the empty container. Countries with such schemes typically collect a much higher share of their bottles and cans than countries relying only on household recycling bins, and the returned containers are cleaner and easier to recycle. Retailers must find space for return machines or counters, which can be difficult for small shops. For this reason, some schemes exempt the smallest shops from taking back containers, while still requiring them to charge the deposit.

passages.title: Free public transport
passages.text: A few towns and cities have made local public transport free for everyone. Where this has been tried, the number of passengers has usually risen. Studies show, however, that many of the new passengers previously walked or cycled, while fewer gave up their cars. The cost of free transport, which must be covered from other public funds, is also significant: fares often pay for a large part of a network's running costs. Supporters argue that free transport has social benefits beyond reducing car use, such as making it easier for people on low incomes to reach jobs and services.

passages.title: Short-term rentals
passages.text: Online platforms have made it easy for owners to rent out flats to tourists for a few nights at a time. In popular city centres, residents have complained about noise, suitcases in stairwells and a sense that their neighbourhoods are emptying of permanent residents. Several cities now require owners to register short-term rentals, and some limit the number of nights a whole flat can be rented out each year. Enforcement is a challenge, because many listings are not registered. Some cities have therefore reached agreements under which platforms remove listings that do not show a valid registration number.

passages.title: Collecting old textiles
passages.text: Large amounts of clothing and household textiles are thrown away with general waste each year. To change this, rules in a number of countries now require separate collection of used textiles, for example through bins at recycling centres. Collection, however, is only the first step. Items in good condition can be sold again, but much of what is collected is too worn for reuse, and the technology to turn old fabrics, especially mixed fibres, into new ones is still limited. Critics warn that without more recycling capacity, separately collected textiles may simply be exported or burned.

passages.title: Vertical farms
passages.text: Vertical farms grow plants indoors in stacked layers under artificial light, often without soil. Because conditions are controlled, they use far less water than open fields and need no pesticides, and they can be built close to the cities where the food is eaten. The main drawback is energy: lighting and climate control make up a large share of their costs. For this reason, most vertical farms grow fast-growing, high-value crops such as salad leaves and herbs rather than staple crops such as wheat. Several companies in the sector have closed in recent years after energy prices rose.

passages.title: Citizens' assemblies
passages.text: A citizens' assembly brings together a group of people chosen at random to discuss a policy question, such as how to reduce emissions. Members hear from experts, deliberate over several weekends and then make recommendations. Supporters say that random selection produces a group that reflects the wider population better than those who usually take part in public debates. Critics point out that the recommendations are not binding, and that governments have sometimes adopted only a small number of them. Organisers stress that assemblies work best when the government states in advance how it will respond to the recommendations.

passages.title: Remote medical consultations
passages.text: Consultations with a doctor by phone or video have become a common part of health care. Patients value not having to travel or take time off work, and the approach can help people in remote areas. Doctors note, however, that some conditions cannot be assessed properly without a physical examination, and that it is easier to miss warning signs at a distance. Older patients and those without a reliable internet connection may also find remote consultations harder to use. Most health services therefore offer remote consultations alongside, not instead of, appointments in person.

passages.title: Grazing against wildfires
passages.text: In some fire-prone regions, authorities pay shepherds to graze goats and sheep on land where dry vegetation builds up. By eating grass and shrubs, the animals reduce the amount of fuel available to a fire. The approach is cheaper than clearing land by machine and can reach steep slopes where machines cannot work. It also helps to keep traditional pastoral farming alive in areas where young people have moved away. Grazing alone cannot prevent large fires in extreme weather, however, and experts see it as one tool among several, alongside firebreaks and controlled burning.

passages.title: Moving freight by rail
passages.text: Moving goods by rail instead of by lorry produces far lower emissions for each tonne carried over long distances. Despite this, rail's share of freight transport has hardly grown in many countries. Operators point to several obstacles: rail lines are often busy with passenger trains, which usually take priority, and border crossings can involve changes of locomotive and staff because of different technical and safety rules. For short distances, the time needed to move goods between lorries and trains can cancel out rail's advantages. Investment in longer freight trains and faster transfer terminals is intended to address some of these problems.

passages.title: Smart electricity meters
passages.text: Smart meters record electricity use and send the readings automatically to the supplier, ending the need for estimated bills. They also make it possible to charge different prices at different times of day, so that households can save money by running appliances when demand is low. Studies suggest that the meters on their own lead to only small savings, unless households receive clear information about their use or are on a tariff that rewards shifting it. Some consumers have raised privacy concerns, because detailed readings can reveal when people are at home.

passages.title: Volunteer firefighters
passages.text: In many rural areas, fire services depend largely on volunteers who are called out by pager or phone from their homes and workplaces. The number of volunteers has been falling, as fewer people both live and work in the same village and employers are less willing to let staff leave during working hours. Some regions now offer volunteers small payments, pension points or training that also counts towards other qualifications. Others are encouraging more women and newcomers to join, as volunteers have traditionally been recruited mainly among local men. Professional crews can cover only some of the gap, mainly near larger towns.

passages.title: Training older workers
passages.text: As people work later in life, employers are under pressure to keep the skills of older staff up to date. Surveys show, however, that workers over fifty take part in job-related training less often than younger colleagues. Some of the gap reflects employers' reluctance to invest in staff who may retire within a few years, and some reflects older workers' own doubts about whether training is worth it. Programmes that have succeeded in reaching older workers tend to be short, closely linked to their current job, and offered during working hours rather than in their own time.

passages.title: Childcare and work
passages.text: The cost and availability of childcare strongly influence whether parents of young children, especially mothers, return to paid work. In countries where childcare is expensive, many parents find that a large part of a second salary would go on fees. Several governments have introduced price caps or free hours for young children. Early results show more parents taking up places, but also waiting lists where the number of places has not grown at the same rate. Childcare providers warn that recruiting enough trained staff is the main obstacle to expanding provision.

passages.title: Heat from data centres
passages.text: Data centres, which house the computers behind online services, produce large amounts of heat that is usually released into the air. Some operators now pass this heat to district heating networks, which use it to warm nearby homes and offices. The arrangement works best where a heating network already exists close to the data centre and where demand for heat is steady through the year. Because data centre heat is often at a fairly low temperature, heat pumps are usually needed to raise it before use. Some local authorities now require new data centres to examine whether their heat can be reused.

passages.title: Reusable food containers
passages.text: Some cities are testing schemes in which takeaway food is served in reusable containers that customers return to any participating restaurant. A deposit or an app account encourages people to bring the containers back. Pilot schemes have found that the environmental benefit depends on how many times each container is used: a reusable box must make many trips before it has a smaller footprint than single-use packaging, because it is heavier to produce and must be washed. Return rates have varied widely between schemes, and have generally been higher where many restaurants in a small area take part.

passages.title: Digital identity wallets
passages.text: Several countries are developing digital identity wallets: phone apps that store an official identity document and other credentials, such as a driving licence or a diploma. Users could prove who they are online, or share only one detail, such as being over eighteen, without revealing their full identity. Supporters argue that this would make online public services easier to use and reduce the need to copy paper documents. Critics raise concerns about security and about people who do not have a smartphone. Most plans therefore keep traditional documents available, and make the use of a wallet voluntary.

passages.title: Charging for plastic bags
passages.text: Many countries now require shops to charge for single-use plastic carrier bags rather than give them away. Where a charge has been introduced, the number of bags handed out has usually fallen sharply within the first year. Some of the effect comes from shoppers reusing bags they already own, and some from a switch to paper or heavier plastic bags. Because these alternatives require more material to make, their environmental benefit depends on being reused several times. For this reason, some countries charge for all carrier bags, not only the thinnest plastic ones.

passages.title: Night mayors
passages.text: Several cities have appointed a 'night mayor': an official who represents the interests of the night-time economy, from bars and music venues to late-shift workers. The role is usually advisory. Night mayors try to settle disputes between venues and residents over noise, and push for better late-night public transport. Supporters say the night economy brings jobs and tourism but has long been treated only as a problem for the police. Residents' groups are more cautious, arguing that the interests of people trying to sleep should carry at least as much weight as those of venues.

passages.title: Seed banks
passages.text: Seed banks store samples of seeds at low temperatures so that they remain alive for decades. They protect crop varieties that are no longer widely grown, which may carry traits useful to future plant breeders, such as resistance to drought or disease. Some banks keep duplicate samples in other countries in case their own collections are damaged. Storage alone does not keep every variety usable, however: seeds slowly lose their ability to germinate, so samples must be tested regularly and grown again to produce fresh seed. This work requires land, staff and long-term funding.

passages.title: Learning accounts
passages.text: Some governments have introduced individual learning accounts: a sum of money credited to each adult that can be spent on approved training courses. The idea is to give people control over their own training, rather than relying on employers to decide who is trained. Early experience shows that the accounts are used most by people who already have higher qualifications, while those with fewer qualifications use them less. Some schemes have responded by giving a larger credit to people with lower qualifications and by offering advice on choosing a course. Quality control is also a concern, as some providers have offered courses of little value.

passages.title: Light pollution
passages.text: Artificial light at night makes the sky over towns several times brighter than it would be naturally. Besides hiding the stars, it can disturb insects, birds that migrate at night, and the sleep patterns of people. Some local authorities have responded by dimming street lights after midnight, switching them off on quiet roads, or replacing them with lamps that direct light downwards and use warmer colours. Residents have sometimes objected that dimmer streets feel less safe, although studies of the effect on crime have so far given mixed results.

passages.title: Free school meals
passages.text: Some regions provide a free lunch to every primary school pupil, regardless of family income. Supporters argue that offering meals to all removes the stigma attached to free meals for poorer children and ensures that children who are not eligible under income rules, but still go hungry, are reached. The cost is considerably higher than for meals limited to low-income families. Schools taking part also need adequate kitchens and dining space, which not all of them had when the scheme began. Some evaluations report better concentration in afternoon lessons, although results differ between studies.

passages.title: Trucks without diesel
passages.text: Manufacturers are developing heavy trucks powered by batteries or by hydrogen to replace diesel models. Battery trucks are already used for regional deliveries, where they can return to a depot to recharge each night. For long-distance haulage, their weight and charging time remain obstacles, and some manufacturers see hydrogen as the better option over long distances. Hydrogen trucks can be refuelled quickly, but very few refuelling stations exist yet, and producing hydrogen without fossil fuels is still expensive. Most observers expect both technologies to be used, for different kinds of journeys.

passages.title: Preprints in science
passages.text: Researchers increasingly post their papers online as 'preprints' before they have been checked by other scientists through peer review. This allows findings to be shared quickly, which proved valuable during public health emergencies. The drawback is that preprints may contain errors that peer review would have caught, and some have been reported in the media as if they were established results. Many preprint servers now display a warning that the work has not been reviewed. Journals generally still accept papers that have first appeared as preprints.

passages.title: Free museum days
passages.text: Many museums offer free entry on certain days, such as the first Sunday of each month. Visitor numbers on free days are usually much higher than on paid days. Surveys suggest, however, that a large share of free-day visitors are people who already visit museums regularly, rather than first-time visitors from groups that rarely go to museums. Some museums have therefore combined free days with outreach work, such as visits for local schools and community groups. Museum staff also report that very crowded free days can make visits less enjoyable for everyone.

passages.title: Hedgerows on farms
passages.text: Hedgerows, the lines of shrubs and trees that divide fields, provide food and shelter for insects, birds and small mammals, and help to reduce soil erosion. In many regions large lengths of hedgerow were removed in the second half of the twentieth century to create bigger fields suited to modern machinery. Several countries now pay farmers to plant new hedgerows or to manage existing ones less intensively, for example by cutting them every other year instead of every year. A newly planted hedgerow takes several years to provide the full benefits of a mature one.

passages.title: Car-free city centres
passages.text: A number of cities have closed parts of their centres to most private cars, while allowing access for residents, deliveries at set times, emergency vehicles and people with disabilities. Air quality and noise in the closed streets have generally improved. Retailers often fear a loss of customers before a closure, but results afterwards have been mixed, with some streets gaining footfall and others losing it. Traffic on surrounding roads may increase, at least at first. Cities that combine closures with better public transport and parking at the edge of the centre report the least opposition.

passages.title: Refurbished phones
passages.text: Refurbished smartphones are used devices that have been checked, repaired where needed and resold, usually with a warranty. They cost considerably less than new models, and buying one avoids the emissions and raw materials involved in making a new phone. The market has grown, but some buyers remain wary about battery condition and how long the phone will continue to receive software updates. Some sellers now grade devices by their cosmetic condition and state the battery's remaining capacity, which helps buyers compare offers.

passages.title: Machine translation in administrations
passages.text: Public administrations that work in several languages increasingly use machine translation to produce first drafts. Translators then revise the drafts, which can be faster than translating from scratch when the text is routine. For legal texts and documents where precise wording matters, administrations generally still require full human translation or very careful revision. Translators report that revising machine output demands a different kind of attention, as errors can be fluent and therefore easy to overlook. Some administrations limit machine translation to internal documents and keep it away from texts published for citizens.

passages.title: Leaking water pipes
passages.text: In many water networks, a significant share of treated drinking water is lost through leaking pipes before it reaches consumers. Replacing old pipes is expensive and disruptive, as it usually means digging up roads. Water companies therefore also use methods to find and repair the largest leaks, such as acoustic sensors that detect the sound of escaping water, and reduce pressure in the network at night, when demand is low, to lower losses. Regulators in some countries set targets for reducing leakage and can impose penalties on companies that miss them.

passages.title: Community energy
passages.text: In community energy projects, local residents jointly own and invest in renewable energy installations, such as solar panels on public buildings or a small wind turbine. Profits are shared among members or reinvested locally. Supporters say local ownership increases acceptance of new installations, since people who benefit directly are less likely to oppose them. The projects often depend on volunteers with technical and financial knowledge, and many struggle with the complexity of connecting to the grid and raising capital. Some countries reserve a share of support schemes for community projects.

passages.title: Town twinning
passages.text: Since the mid-twentieth century, thousands of towns in Europe have formed partnerships with towns in other countries, known as twinning. Partnerships typically involve exchange visits by schools, sports clubs and cultural groups. In many places activity has declined as the volunteers who ran the exchanges have grown older and fewer young people have taken over. Some twinning associations have revived their partnerships by organising joint projects online and by focusing on shared practical issues, such as local responses to climate change.

passages.title: Phones in schools
passages.text: A growing number of schools restrict pupils' use of mobile phones during the school day, either by banning them entirely or by requiring them to be kept in lockers or pouches. Supporters argue that fewer distractions improve concentration and reduce online bullying during school hours. Evidence on the effect on results is so far limited and mixed. Some parents are concerned about not being able to contact their children, while teachers point out that phones can also be useful learning tools when their use is planned. Many schools therefore allow phones in particular lessons.

passages.title: Ageing bridges
passages.text: Many road bridges in Europe were built in the decades after 1950 and were not designed for today's traffic, especially the number and weight of heavy lorries. Engineers inspect bridges at regular intervals, but inspection budgets have not always kept pace with the growing number of ageing structures. When a bridge is found to be weak, authorities may reduce the weight limit, close a lane, or close the bridge entirely while repairs are planned. Such closures can cause long diversions for traffic. Some authorities are installing sensors that monitor bridges continuously between inspections.

passages.title: Online dispute resolution
passages.text: When consumers have a dispute with a trader over an online purchase, going to court is often too slow and costly for the amounts involved. Alternative dispute resolution bodies offer a cheaper way to settle such disputes, usually through mediation or a decision by an independent expert. Participation is voluntary for traders in many sectors, which limits the reach of these bodies. Consumers are also often unaware that they exist. Where traders do take part, most cases are settled faster than they would be in court.

passages.title: Green roofs
passages.text: Green roofs are covered with plants growing in a layer of soil or another growing medium. They hold back rainwater, which reduces the risk of drains overflowing during heavy storms, and they can lower the temperature of the building below in summer. They also provide habitat for insects and birds. A green roof needs a structure strong enough to bear the extra weight, which can make it difficult to add one to an existing building. Some cities require green roofs on new flat-roofed buildings above a certain size.

passages.title: Removing old dams
passages.text: Across Europe, many small dams and weirs built for mills, irrigation or flood control are no longer used. They block the movement of fish such as salmon and eels, and trap sediment that would otherwise move downstream. Some authorities have begun removing obsolete barriers, and monitoring after removal has often recorded fish returning upstream within a few years. Removal is not always welcomed: some residents value the ponds created behind old dams, and in some places the structures are protected as heritage. Each case therefore requires an assessment of the benefits and the local objections.

passages.title: Public toilets
passages.text: The number of public toilets in many towns has fallen as local authorities have cut costs. The lack of toilets particularly affects older people, people with certain medical conditions, parents with young children and outdoor workers, some of whom say they avoid going out for long periods as a result. Some towns have responded with schemes in which cafés and shops let non-customers use their toilets in return for a small payment from the council. Such schemes cost less than running public facilities, but the toilets are available only during the businesses' opening hours.

passages.title: Subsidies for e-bikes
passages.text: Several cities and regions offer grants towards the purchase of electric bicycles. The aim is to replace car journeys, since e-bikes make longer distances and hilly routes manageable for more people. Surveys of grant recipients suggest that many do use their e-bikes instead of a car for some trips, especially commuting. However, some recipients say they would have bought an e-bike anyway, which means part of the grant money has no effect on behaviour. Some schemes therefore target groups considered less likely to buy without help, such as people on lower incomes.

passages.title: Surplus food
passages.text: Supermarkets throw away food that is close to its date or has damaged packaging but is still safe to eat. In some countries, large supermarkets are now required to offer such food to charities instead of discarding it. Food banks have welcomed the extra supply, but say that they need more refrigerated storage and transport to handle fresh products, which spoil quickly. Charities also point out that donated surplus varies from day to day, which makes it difficult to plan balanced food parcels.

passages.title: Salaries in job adverts
passages.text: Some countries now require employers to state the salary or a salary range in job advertisements. Supporters argue that this helps applicants decide whether to apply and helps to reduce unexplained pay differences, including between men and women. Employers' groups have warned that publishing salaries could make it harder to negotiate with exceptional candidates and could cause discontent among existing staff. Early studies of such rules suggest that applicants respond positively to adverts that state a salary, though the effect on pay differences will take longer to measure.

passages.title: Wind turbines and birds
passages.text: Wind turbines can kill birds and bats that collide with the rotating blades. The risk varies greatly with the location of a wind farm: turbines on migration routes or near breeding colonies of large birds pose a much higher risk than those elsewhere. Careful choice of sites is therefore considered the most effective measure. Some operators also stop turbines when radar or cameras detect birds approaching, or at times of peak migration. Studies of one method, painting one blade black to make the rotor more visible, have reported fewer collisions, but it has so far been tested at only a few sites.

passages.title: Parking without cash
passages.text: Many towns have removed coins from parking meters, asking drivers to pay by card or by smartphone app instead. Councils say this cuts the cost of collecting cash and reduces theft from meters. Motorists' groups have criticised the change, saying that drivers without a smartphone or a bank card are excluded, and that some apps charge an extra fee for each payment. Some towns have kept a small number of cash-accepting machines or allow payment in nearby shops. Others have kept coin payment in car parks used mainly by older visitors.

passages.title: Air conditioning
passages.text: The use of air conditioning in European homes has increased as summers have become hotter. Air conditioning protects health during heat waves, especially for older people, but it uses electricity and releases heat into the street outside, which can make cities warmer still. Experts recommend reducing the need for cooling first, for example through external shading, better insulation and opening windows at night. Heat pumps that both heat and cool a home are generally more efficient than older air-conditioning units.

passages.title: Coworking in villages
passages.text: As more people work from home for part of the week, some villages and small towns have opened shared offices, or coworking spaces, often in former schools, shops or railway stations. They offer a reliable internet connection, a desk and the company of other workers, which many remote workers miss at home. Organisers hope the spaces will encourage people to move to or stay in rural areas. Many spaces depend on public start-up funding, and some have closed when it ended because too few people paid for regular use.

passages.title: Night flights
passages.text: Aircraft noise at night disturbs the sleep of people living near airports and has been linked to health effects. Several airports therefore restrict night flights, either by banning them during certain hours or by limiting the number of flights and the noise level of the aircraft allowed. Airlines and freight operators argue that restrictions reduce connectivity and can move business to airports with fewer limits. Some airports use charges that make night landings more expensive for noisier aircraft, encouraging airlines to use quieter models at night.

passages.title: Allotment gardens
passages.text: Allotments are small plots of land rented out, usually by local authorities or associations, for people to grow their own fruit and vegetables. Demand has risen in many towns, and waiting lists can run to several years. Some authorities have responded by dividing large plots into smaller ones, which also suits tenants with less time. Plot holders say the gardens bring benefits beyond food, including exercise and contact with neighbours. In some places allotment land has been sold for housing, which plot holders' associations have opposed.

passages.title: Training against phishing
passages.text: Phishing emails try to trick people into clicking harmful links or revealing passwords. Many organisations train staff by sending simulated phishing emails and showing those who click how to spot the warning signs. Click rates in such tests usually fall after training. Security experts warn, however, that training cannot remove the risk entirely, since well-crafted messages can deceive even careful staff. They recommend combining training with technical measures, such as two-step login, so that a stolen password alone is not enough to break in.

passages.title: Fishing quotas
passages.text: To prevent overfishing, catches of many fish species are limited by annual quotas based on scientific estimates of the size of each stock. Where quotas have followed scientific advice, a number of stocks that were once severely depleted have recovered. In other cases, quotas have been set above the recommended level to limit the immediate impact on fishing communities, which has slowed recovery. Scientists also note that stocks are affected by factors beyond fishing, such as rising sea temperatures, which make estimates less certain.

passages.title: Repairability scores
passages.text: Some countries require certain electronic products, such as smartphones and washing machines, to display a repairability score at the point of sale. The score reflects factors such as how easily the device can be taken apart, how long spare parts remain available and how much they cost. Supporters hope the score will lead buyers to choose more repairable products and push manufacturers to improve them. Early data show that the average scores of some product types have risen since the scores were introduced. It is less clear how much the scores influence what consumers actually buy.

passages.title: Who will take over the farm?
passages.text: A large share of farmers in Europe are over sixty, while relatively few are under forty. When farmers retire, many farms have no family member willing to take over, and the land may be sold to larger farms or for other uses. Young people who want to farm but do not come from farming families often struggle to obtain land and the capital needed to start. Some regions offer start-up grants, and some programmes match retiring farmers with new entrants who are not relatives, allowing a gradual handover over several years.

passages.title: Open-plan offices
passages.text: Many organisations have moved staff from individual offices into open-plan spaces, partly to save space and partly in the hope of encouraging collaboration. Several studies, however, have found that face-to-face conversations can decrease after such a move, as staff turn to email and messaging to avoid being overheard. Noise and interruptions are the most common complaints. Some organisations now provide quiet rooms and small meeting booths alongside open areas, so that staff can choose a space to suit each task.

passages.title: Snow at ski resorts
passages.text: Warmer winters have shortened the snow season at many lower-altitude ski resorts. Many resorts rely on artificial snow, which requires large amounts of water and energy and works only when temperatures are low enough. Some resorts at lower altitudes have closed, while others are developing activities for all seasons, such as hiking and mountain biking, to reduce their dependence on winter sports. Resorts at higher altitudes are generally less affected so far.

passages.title: Health care abroad
passages.text: Patients may in some cases seek treatment in another EU country and have the costs reimbursed by their own health system. Reimbursement is usually limited to what the treatment would have cost at home, and for some treatments, such as those requiring an overnight hospital stay, prior authorisation may be required. Relatively few patients use this option. Reasons include a lack of awareness, the need to pay upfront and wait for reimbursement, and language barriers. Patients living near a border are among those most likely to use it.

passages.title: Bicycle theft
passages.text: Bicycle theft discourages people from cycling: some victims do not buy another bicycle, and others buy cheaper models they mind less about losing. Few stolen bicycles are returned to their owners, partly because owners rarely record frame numbers. Some cities offer free registration, engraving a code on the frame and recording it in a database that the police can check. Secure bicycle parking at stations and in residential streets is also expanding, although demand often exceeds the spaces available.

passages.title: Tap water in restaurants
passages.text: In some countries, restaurants are required to provide tap water free of charge or for a small service fee when customers ask for it. Supporters argue that this reduces plastic waste from bottled water and makes drinking water accessible to everyone. Some restaurant owners object that selling bottled water is a significant source of income. Where public drinking water is safe, it is subject to strict quality controls, and studies have found that it is often of similar quality to bottled water at a far lower cost.

passages.title: Trees against urban heat
passages.text: Street trees can lower the temperature of the air and of pavements beneath them on hot days, through shade and the evaporation of water from their leaves. Many cities have therefore set targets for increasing the share of their area covered by tree canopy. Planting is only the start: young trees need regular watering for several years, and many die during their first dry summers. Space is also a constraint, since pipes and cables under pavements limit where large trees can grow. Some cities now plan tree planting together with street repairs to make room for roots.

passages.title: Parcel lockers
passages.text: Parcel lockers allow online shoppers to collect deliveries at a time that suits them, from banks of lockers at stations, supermarkets and petrol stations. For delivery companies, dropping many parcels at one locker is quicker than delivering to individual homes, and avoids failed deliveries when nobody is in. Studies suggest the environmental benefit depends on how customers reach the lockers: walking or collecting on an existing journey saves emissions, but a special car trip can cancel out the benefit. Some cities are pushing for lockers open to all delivery companies, rather than separate lockers for each.

passages.title: Counting insects
passages.text: Long-term studies in several European countries have recorded large declines in the number of flying insects over recent decades. The causes are thought to include the loss of habitat, the use of pesticides and changes in climate, although their relative importance is debated. Monitoring insects is difficult because numbers vary greatly from year to year with the weather, so trends become clear only over many years. Several countries have set up national monitoring programmes, some of which rely on trained volunteers to collect and identify samples.

passages.title: Second homes
passages.text: In some rural and coastal areas, a large share of houses are second homes, occupied only for part of the year. Owners bring spending to local businesses during their stays. Local residents, however, often find themselves priced out of the housing market, and villages can feel empty out of season, putting pressure on shops and schools. Some regions have responded with higher property taxes on second homes or with rules reserving new housing for people who live or work locally. Owners' associations argue that such measures discourage investment in the areas concerned.

passages.title: Recruiting nurses abroad
passages.text: Many European health services face a shortage of nurses and have recruited staff from other countries. International recruitment can fill vacancies quickly, but it raises questions about the effect on the countries the nurses leave, some of which also face shortages. International guidelines discourage active recruitment from countries with the most severe shortages. Recruited nurses often need language training and recognition of their qualifications before they can work at their full level, which can take many months. Health services are also trying to train more nurses at home and to keep existing staff from leaving.

passages.title: Energy ratings for buildings
passages.text: When a building is sold or rented in the EU, an energy performance certificate rating its energy efficiency must normally be provided. The ratings are intended to help buyers and tenants compare running costs and to encourage owners to improve their buildings. Studies suggest that better-rated homes tend to sell or rent for higher prices, although other factors such as location matter more. Critics point out that certificates are sometimes based on brief inspections and may not reflect how much energy a building actually uses, which depends partly on the behaviour of the people living in it.

passages.title: Charging electric cars
passages.text: Most charging of electric cars takes place at home or at work, where drivers can plug in for hours at a time. Drivers without a private driveway, such as many people in city flats, depend more on public charging points, which are generally more expensive per unit of electricity. Local authorities have installed chargers in residential streets, sometimes built into lampposts. Fast chargers on motorways are important for long journeys, although they account for a smaller share of total charging. Surveys suggest that worries about finding a charger remain a reason some people hesitate to buy an electric car.

passages.title: Less salt in food
passages.text: Most of the salt people eat comes not from the salt shaker but from processed foods such as bread, ready meals and cheese. Several countries have agreed targets with food producers to reduce the salt content of these products step by step, so that consumers adjust to the taste gradually. Where such programmes have been closely monitored, the salt content of many products has fallen. Progress has been uneven, however, and some producers have not met the targets. Health organisations argue that voluntary targets should be backed by rules if progress stalls.

passages.title: Libraries of things
passages.text: A 'library of things' lends household items that people need only occasionally, such as drills, ladders, sewing machines and camping gear, in return for a small fee or membership. The idea is to save money and reduce waste, since many such items are used only a few times in their lifetime. Some are run by volunteers, others by public libraries. Organisers report that the most popular items are tools for home repairs and gardening. Keeping items in working order and replacing broken ones are ongoing costs that fees rarely cover in full.

passages.title: Empty shops
passages.text: Many town centres have a growing number of empty shops, as more shopping moves online and to out-of-town retail parks. Empty units can make a high street feel neglected, which in turn discourages visitors. Some towns now allow temporary use of empty shops by artists, start-up businesses or community groups, often at low rent, until a long-term tenant is found. Such arrangements can bring life back to a street, but they depend on the willingness of property owners, some of whom prefer to wait for a tenant paying full rent.

passages.title: Reusing treated wastewater
passages.text: In regions where water is scarce, treated wastewater can be used to irrigate crops instead of being discharged into rivers or the sea. Water for irrigation must meet quality standards that depend on the type of crop, with the strictest standards for crops eaten raw. Reuse can relieve pressure on rivers and groundwater during droughts. It requires additional treatment and pipes to carry the water to farms, which increases costs. Public acceptance has also been a concern, although surveys suggest it grows when people understand how the water is treated.

passages.title: Ombudsmen
passages.text: An ombudsman investigates complaints from members of the public about the way public authorities have dealt with them, for example delays, unfair treatment or failure to follow procedures. Using an ombudsman is free, and complainants are usually expected first to raise the issue with the authority concerned. An ombudsman cannot overturn a decision in the way a court can, but can recommend that an authority apologise, reconsider a case or change its procedures. Most authorities follow such recommendations, partly because ombudsmen publish their findings.

passages.title: Collecting food waste
passages.text: A growing number of local authorities collect food waste separately from other household rubbish, usually in small caddies emptied every week. The collected waste can be turned into compost or into biogas, which can be used to generate energy. Separate collection also reduces the amount of waste sent to landfill or incineration. Participation varies, however: some households find the caddies inconvenient or are put off by smells, especially in summer. Authorities that provide free compostable liners and collect frequently tend to report higher participation.

passages.title: Mentoring new teachers
passages.text: A significant share of new teachers leave the profession within their first few years. Many education systems now assign each new teacher an experienced colleague as a mentor during their first year or two. Studies suggest that mentoring is associated with higher retention, particularly when mentors teach the same subject and have time set aside for the role. Where mentors must fit mentoring around a full teaching load, the support is often limited to occasional conversations. Some schools also give new teachers a lighter timetable in their first year.

passages.title: Crossings for wildlife
passages.text: Roads and railways divide the habitats of many animals and cause collisions that kill wildlife and endanger drivers. Wildlife crossings, such as green bridges over roads and tunnels beneath them, allow animals to cross safely. Monitoring with cameras has recorded deer, foxes, badgers and many smaller animals using such crossings. Crossings work best when combined with fences that guide animals towards them. Green bridges are expensive, so tunnels and adapted culverts are more common, particularly for smaller species.

passages.title: Sign language interpreting
passages.text: Deaf people who use sign language often depend on interpreters to communicate in health care, education and dealings with public services. In many countries there are too few qualified interpreters, so appointments have to be booked well in advance. Remote interpreting, in which an interpreter joins by video, has made interpreters easier to reach at short notice. Deaf associations welcome remote interpreting as an addition, but note that it is not suitable for every situation, for example when a person is unwell or a video connection is poor.

passages.title: Automated border gates
passages.text: Many airports now offer automated border gates, where travellers scan their passport and have their face compared with the passport photo by a camera. The gates can process passengers faster than manual checks and allow border guards to focus on more complex cases. They are generally limited to adults with biometric passports, and families with young children are usually directed to staffed desks. When the gates fail to match a traveller, the traveller is referred to a border guard. Data protection rules govern how the images taken at the gates may be stored.

passages.title: Micro-credentials
passages.text: Micro-credentials certify the learning gained from short courses, such as a few weeks of training in data analysis or project management. They allow people to update their skills without enrolling in a full degree. Employers' recognition of micro-credentials varies, partly because the quality and content of courses differ widely between providers. Several initiatives aim to make them easier to compare, for example by describing each credential's workload, level and how learning was assessed in a standard format.

passages.title: The return of the tram
passages.text: Many European cities removed their tram networks in the mid-twentieth century in favour of buses and cars. Since the 1980s, a number of cities have built new tram lines. Trams can carry more passengers than buses and are often seen as more attractive by travellers, which can draw people out of cars. Construction is costly and disruptive, however, and requires space on busy streets. In smaller cities, some authorities have chosen high-quality bus services with dedicated lanes instead, which provide some of the same benefits at lower cost.

passages.title: Counting birds in gardens
passages.text: In some countries, members of the public are invited to count the birds in their garden or local park for an hour on a set weekend each year and submit the results online. Hundreds of thousands of people take part. Because the same method is used each year, the results help scientists to track changes in common bird populations across the country. Organisers acknowledge that volunteers may misidentify some species, but they argue that the large number of participants makes the overall trends reliable. The counts also raise public interest in wildlife.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Most evaluations of the zones have concentrated on air quality.
wrong: The zones have reduced the total amount of traffic in these cities.
Every city with a zone offers grants for a replacement vehicle.
Nitrogen dioxide fell in the districts around the zones.
questions.explanation: The passage says evaluations 'have focused mainly on air quality'. It reports a claim that traffic moves elsewhere, not a fall in total traffic; it says only 'some' cities offer grants; and it mentions falls in nitrogen dioxide along major roads, not in surrounding districts.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Office space decisions rarely rest on evidence about productivity.
wrong: Shared desks have made staff less productive.
Most administrations have given up whole floors of their buildings.
Office buildings are busiest on Mondays and Fridays.
questions.explanation: Few organisations have measured productivity, so decisions rest 'largely on the basis of cost and staff preferences'. Nothing is said about shared desks lowering productivity, the passage does not say how many gave up floors, and buildings are almost empty on Mondays and Fridays.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Properly stored pasta can be safe to eat after its 'best before' date.
wrong: Fresh fish can be eaten after its 'use by' date if it smells fine.
Most consumers understand the difference between the two labels.
Food past its 'best before' date has usually lost all its flavour.
questions.explanation: After a 'best before' date, food such as pasta 'is still safe if it has been stored properly'. Food past its 'use by' date should not be eaten even if it smells fine, surveys suggest many consumers do not know the difference, and the passage says food 'may lose some flavour', not all of it.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: A large set of identical responses is usually counted as one.
wrong: Online consultations reflect the views of the wider public.
Panels of randomly selected citizens have replaced online consultations.
Online consultations are open only to organisations.
questions.explanation: Identical responses 'are usually treated as a single organised campaign rather than counted individually'. The passage says responses may not reflect the wider public, panels are used alongside consultations rather than instead of them, and consultations are open to anyone with an internet connection.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Sleeping cars hold fewer passengers than seated carriages.
wrong: Night trains are most popular on routes shorter than 800 kilometres.
All the new night train routes are run without public support.
Night trains were never withdrawn from European routes.
questions.explanation: The passage states that 'sleeping cars carry fewer passengers than seated carriages'. Demand is strongest between 800 and 1,500 kilometres, several routes depend on public support, and many services were withdrawn in the early 2000s.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Mowing less often can save councils money.
wrong: Councils have stopped mowing their parks altogether.
All residents support leaving the grass uncut.
The mown strips are meant to provide food for insects.
questions.explanation: Councils report 'lower maintenance costs, as fewer cuts are needed'. They still cut once or twice a year, some residents object, and the mown strips show that the grass was left long deliberately; it is the wild flowers that feed insects.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: A library may have to pay again for an e-book it already offers.
wrong: Printed books are licensed to libraries for two years.
Publishers want libraries to lend e-books without limits.
All countries have national agreements on e-book prices.
questions.explanation: Licences expire after a fixed period or number of loans, 'after which the library must pay again'. It is e-books, not printed books, that are licensed; publishers worry that unlimited lending could reduce sales; and only 'some countries' have begun negotiating national agreements.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Missing spare parts can prevent a repair.
wrong: Visitors pay a small fee for each repair.
Visitors are not expected to help with the repair.
Organisers keep no record of what is repaired.
questions.explanation: Spare parts that are no longer sold are among 'the most common obstacles' to a repair. The events are free, visitors are expected to take part in the repair, and organisers record what is brought in and whether it was fixed.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: One argument against changing the clocks is its effect on sleep.
wrong: Studies show that changing the clocks saves large amounts of energy.
All European countries have agreed to stay on summer time.
Lighting now accounts for a larger share of energy use than before.
questions.explanation: Critics 'point to disrupted sleep in the days after each change'. Studies suggest the energy savings are small, the passage describes a choice each country would still have to make, and lighting now accounts for a smaller share of energy use.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
questions.correct: Plain-language letters can cut queries and still include legal details.
wrong: Plain language means removing legal details from official letters.
Rewriting standard letters is too expensive for most administrations.
Readers prefer letters with long sentences and legal terms.
questions.explanation: The trials led to fewer calls and more replies on time, and legal details 'can still be included'. The passage says the opposite of removing legal details, officials say the cost is recovered, and nothing suggests readers prefer long legal sentences.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Scooter trips that replace walking do little to cut traffic emissions.
wrong: All cities now require scooters to be parked in marked bays.
Most scooter trips are longer than three kilometres.
Cities were consulted before the scooters appeared on their streets.
questions.explanation: Many trips 'replace walking rather than car journeys, which weakens the claim that scooters significantly cut traffic emissions'. Only some cities require marked bays, most trips are under three kilometres, and the scooters appeared 'with little warning'.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Strawberries are still picked mainly by hand.
wrong: Machines have replaced most seasonal workers on fruit farms.
Employers find it easier than before to recruit seasonal workers.
Workers' organisations want fewer inspections of workers' housing.
questions.explanation: Delicate crops such as strawberries 'are still largely picked by hand'. Only some farms have invested in machines, employers say recruiting has become harder, and workers' organisations call for more regular inspections.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
questions.correct: Managed retreat is now the most common way of protecting coasts.
wrong: Sea walls can make erosion worse elsewhere on the coast.
Salt marshes can reduce the force of waves.
Some people oppose managed retreat because they would lose property.
questions.explanation: Managed retreat has been chosen only 'in a few places', so it is not the most common approach. The other three statements are all in the passage: defences can increase erosion further along the coast, salt marshes absorb wave energy, and people who would lose land or homes oppose managed retreat.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Interpreters usually take turns because the work is so demanding.
wrong: Simultaneous interpretation means translating after the speaker has finished.
Remote interpretation has made interpreters' work less tiring.
Speakers are asked to read their texts as quickly as possible.
questions.explanation: 'The work is so demanding that interpreters normally take turns.' Simultaneous interpretation happens as speech is delivered, interpreters report that remote work can be more tiring, and speakers help by not reading too quickly.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Most of the returning wolves arrived by themselves from nearby areas.
wrong: Wolves were released into the wild in most of the regions concerned.
Farmers receive no support for protecting their animals.
Electric fences are cheap to install on hilly land.
questions.explanation: Wolves returned 'mostly by moving in from neighbouring areas rather than through reintroduction'. Several regions pay compensation and subsidise fences and guard dogs, and fences are costly to install on large or hilly areas.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: In some cities the tax is higher during the busiest season.
wrong: Cities that raised the tax have seen a sharp fall in visitors.
The tax is usually a percentage of the price of a flight.
Short-term rentals are exempt from the tax in every city.
questions.explanation: 'Some cities set higher rates in peak season.' Cities that raised their rates report little effect on visitor numbers, the tax is usually a fixed amount per night added to the hotel bill, and in several cities it also applies to short-term rentals.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
questions.correct: Data are reused more when kept current and easy to use.
wrong: Publishing data online always leads to new apps and services.
Public data should be made available only to researchers.
Most public data sets are sold to businesses.
questions.explanation: The passage says publication alone is not enough and that the most reuse comes from regularly updated, user-led data. It does not say publication always leads to new services, the data are meant for businesses, researchers and citizens, and they are published free of charge.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
questions.correct: Young people are less willing to volunteer than older people.
wrong: Many young volunteers prefer short projects.
Some organisations have split long-term roles into smaller tasks.
questions.explanation: Surveys suggest young people are 'as willing to volunteer as older generations', so this statement is not supported. The other three appear in the passage: many prefer short projects, some organisations have split roles into smaller tasks, and some schools and universities recognise volunteering formally.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Low use is one reason cash machines in rural areas close.
wrong: Retailers all prefer card payments to cash.
Every country requires cash machines within a set distance of most homes.
Cash use has risen since banks closed their branches.
questions.explanation: Closures have happened 'especially in rural areas, where fewer transactions make them less profitable'. Retailers' views are mixed, only some countries have such rules, and the share of cash payments has fallen.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: The organisations in the trials took part by choice.
wrong: Staff in the trials worked fewer hours for less pay.
Hospitals could adopt a four-day week without hiring more staff.
Output fell sharply in most of the trials.
questions.explanation: Critics note that 'the organisations taking part volunteered to do so'. Staff kept the same pay, hospitals would need to hire more people, and in most trials output stayed broadly the same.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Unstaffed hours have so far been added on top of staffed ones.
wrong: Libraries have cut staffed hours to open without staff.
Anyone can use the library during the unstaffed hours.
Unions have welcomed the longer opening hours without reservation.
questions.explanation: The libraries 'have kept their staffed hours unchanged and added the unstaffed hours on top'. Staffed hours have not been cut, only registered users with a library card can enter, and unions have raised concerns.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Shoppers on foot or by bicycle may spend less per visit.
wrong: Protected lanes always increase the takings of nearby shops.
Painted lanes attract more new cyclists than separated ones.
Shopkeepers usually support the removal of parking spaces.
questions.explanation: Such shoppers 'visit more often, even if they spend less on each visit'. Whether this makes up for lost parking 'varies from street to street', the passage does not compare painted lanes with separated ones, and shopkeepers sometimes oppose the lanes because parking is lost.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Employers' organisations worry that a fixed limit could stop low-risk work.
wrong: Employers' organisations reject any protection for outdoor workers.
Every country uses a fixed temperature limit for outdoor work.
Trade unions want each workplace assessed instead of a limit.
questions.explanation: Employers ask for flexibility 'since a fixed temperature limit can stop work even where the risk is low'. They accept the need for protection, only some countries use a limit, and it is the unions who argue for a clear limit.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
questions.correct: Apps help beginners practise, but speaking needs more than an app.
wrong: Apps have replaced language teachers for most learners.
Speech-recognition exercises have solved the problem of speaking practice.
Language apps are of no use to beginners.
questions.explanation: The passage says apps help beginners build vocabulary and a habit, but learners who rely on them alone struggle to speak, so teachers recommend combining them with lessons. Nothing says apps replaced teachers, speech recognition does not always work well, and apps do help beginners.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: Some small shops charge the deposit but take no containers back.
wrong: Small shops are exempt from charging the deposit.
Household recycling bins collect more bottles than deposit schemes.
Containers returned through a deposit scheme are harder to recycle.
questions.explanation: Some schemes exempt the smallest shops from taking back containers 'while still requiring them to charge the deposit'. Deposit schemes collect a much higher share than household bins, and returned containers are cleaner and easier to recycle.

questions.subject: Verbal reasoning
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.correct: A rise in passengers does not mean an equal fall in car use.
wrong: Free transport has mainly attracted former car drivers.
